title: Patterns: worker pool, fan-out/fan-in, pipelines, semaphores, rate limiting
summary: Most concurrent Go programs combine a few shapes: pipelines of stages joined by channels, fan-out to workers and fan-in of their results, a bound on how many things run at once, and a limit on how often they start.

examples.title: A pipeline with fan-out, fan-in and a cancellation path

annotations.note: A stage returns a receive-only channel and starts the goroutine that fills it. That goroutine owns the channel, so it closes it, and downstream range loops end cleanly.
Every send also selects on ctx.Done(). If the consumer stops reading, a plain send would block forever and leak this goroutine; with the select, one cancel() releases it.
Fan-out: three workers range over the same channel and each value goes to exactly one of them. A slow stage gets parallel without any change to the stages around it.

Fan-in needs one extra goroutine that waits for all workers and then closes out. Closing inside a worker would make the others panic on their next send; never closing would leave main's range loop waiting forever.
If main returned early, say on the first bad value, the deferred cancel would unblock every stage still trying to send. Without it, those goroutines would leak.
Workers finish in any order. When order matters, carry an index with each value or write results into a slice by index, as the next example does.

examples.title: Bounding concurrency: worker pool vs semaphore

annotations.note: The tracker only measures concurrency. time.Sleep stands in for I/O so that tasks overlap; nothing here depends on it for ordering.
Each index is written by exactly one goroutine, and wg.Wait orders those writes before the Println, so the slice needs no lock and the results keep input order.

Worker pool: a fixed set of goroutines and one job channel; the concurrency is the number of workers. It suits workers that hold something costly, such as a connection or a large buffer, and reuse it across jobs.

Semaphore: one goroutine per job and a channel of capacity 3 as the gate. The send acquires a slot and blocks while three are taken; the deferred receive releases it. All ten goroutines exist at once, but only three work at a time.

examples.title: Rate limiting: a steady ticker and a token bucket

annotations.note: A loop that waits for a tick before each request can't go faster than the ticker. Only lower bounds on elapsed time are reliable, so that is all the example prints.
The bucket is a buffered channel of tokens. Starting it full lets a burst of three requests through without waiting.

The refill goroutine adds one token per tick and drops it when the bucket is full, so idle time can't bank more than three requests. The done channel stops it; without that, every limiter you create leaks a goroutine and a ticker.
The first three requests take the burst; the next two wait for refills. In production, golang.org/x/time/rate's Limiter.Wait(ctx) does this and lets a waiting request be canceled.

use_cases: Pipeline: parse, enrich, write, e.g. read a CSV export, look up each row, then batch inserts into PostgreSQL
Worker pool: a fixed number of workers, each holding a database connection, processing jobs claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Semaphore: cap concurrent calls to an external API, or concurrent image resizes at the number of cores
Rate limiting: stay under a third-party quota such as 50 requests per second
strengths: Built from language parts (goroutines, channels, select), with no executor framework to configure, unlike Java's ThreadPoolExecutor and its queue and rejection policies
Unbuffered channels give backpressure for free: a fast stage waits for a slow one, where Java's Executors.newFixedThreadPool queues work in an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue
A buffered channel is a semaphore with no extra type, and goroutines are cheap enough that one per item behind a semaphore is a sound design
weaknesses: Every pattern needs a cancellation path and a clear owner for every close. Getting either wrong deadlocks or leaks at run time; the compiler doesn't notice
Fan-out loses order; restoring it means carrying indexes or sequence numbers
No rate limiter in the standard library: bursts, per-key limits and Wait(ctx) come from golang.org/x/time/rate or your own code
Each channel hop is a synchronisation. When the per-item work is tiny, a plain loop can beat a pipeline; measure before splitting cheap work into stages

pitfalls.title: Closing a shared output channel in a worker
pitfalls.detail: The first worker to finish closes it and the others panic with "send on closed channel". Close it from one goroutine after wg.Wait().
pitfalls.bad: wg.Go(func() { for n := range in { out <- n * n }; close(out) })

pitfalls.title: One goroutine per item with no bound
pitfalls.detail: Ten thousand URLs become ten thousand simultaneous connections, file descriptors and memory spikes. Bound it with a pool, a semaphore or errgroup.SetLimit (lesson 6).
pitfalls.bad: for _, u := range urls { go fetch(u) }
pitfalls.good:
g.SetLimit(8)
for _, u := range urls { g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, u) }) }

pitfalls.title: Stages without a cancellation path
pitfalls.detail: When the consumer returns early, every upstream goroutine blocks on its next send forever. Select on ctx.Done() for each send and defer cancel() in the consumer.

pitfalls.title: Rate limiting with time.Sleep
pitfalls.detail: Sleeping after each request makes the rate drift by the request's own duration, and nothing can cancel the sleep. Use a ticker, or rate.Limiter.Wait(ctx).

quiz.q: In a fan-in, who should close the merged output channel?
options: One goroutine that waits for all workers, then closes it
quiz.why: Only after every sender is done is it safe to close; a closing worker would make the others panic on send.

quiz.q: A pipeline's consumer returns after the first bad value. What keeps the upstream goroutines from leaking?
options: Each send also selects on ctx.Done(), and the consumer cancels
quiz.why: Blocked goroutines are never collected. They exit only if something unblocks them, and ctx.Done() is that something.

quiz.q: slots := make(chan struct{}, 3) is used as a semaphore. What does slots <- struct{}{} do when three tokens are already in it?
options: Blocks until another goroutine receives one
quiz.why: A send on a full buffered channel blocks; receiving a token is the release.

further_reading.title: Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation

body:
## Concept

Four shapes cover most concurrent Go code:

- **Pipeline**: stages connected by channels. Each stage is a goroutine that receives
  from its input, does one thing, sends to its output, and closes the output when done.
- **Fan-out / fan-in**: several goroutines read the same channel (fan-out); their
  outputs are merged back into one channel (fan-in).
- **Bounded concurrency**: a **worker pool** (N goroutines pulling from a job channel) or
  a **semaphore** (one goroutine per job, a buffered channel admitting N at a time).
- **Rate limiting**: start work no faster than a fixed rate, with a ticker or a token
  bucket.

The rules that make them safe are the same everywhere: the goroutine that sends on a
channel owns it and closes it, every blocking send also watches `ctx.Done()`, and the
consumer cancels when it stops early.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **C / Unix**: a pipeline is `grep | sort | uniq` inside one process, with channels as
  the pipes and blocking sends as their backpressure.
- **Java**: a worker pool is `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` without the executor:
  the job channel is the queue and `close` is `shutdown()`. A semaphore is
  `java.util.concurrent.Semaphore`.
- **Python**: `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n)` ≈ worker pool; `asyncio.Semaphore` ≈
  the channel semaphore. Goroutines run in parallel, so CPU-bound stages scale across
  cores.
- **JS**: bounding concurrency is what `p-limit` or chunked `Promise.all` do; Node's
  `stream.pipeline` is the pipeline. There, everything shares one thread; here, each
  stage can run on its own core.

## How it works

The pipeline example has this shape:

```
        ┌─► worker 1 ─┐
gen ────┼─► worker 2 ─┼──► out ──► main
        └─► worker 3 ─┘
```

Each value from `gen` goes to exactly one worker, because a receive takes the value off
the channel. The merged `out` must be closed exactly once, after all three workers have
stopped sending, which is why a fourth small goroutine waits on the WaitGroup and then
closes it.

A worker pool and a semaphore bound concurrency the same way, from different ends: the
pool creates N goroutines and feeds them jobs; the semaphore creates one goroutine per
job and lets N through a gate. A third option is `errgroup.Group.SetLimit` (next lesson),
which adds error handling. `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` offers a weighted semaphore
whose `Acquire(ctx, n)` can be canceled.

## Design notes

Start with the simplest thing: a loop. Add a pipeline when stages have different costs
and you want them to overlap, such as reading the next CSV rows while the database
insert of the previous batch is in flight. Add fan-out only to the slow stage.

Prefer a semaphore or `errgroup.SetLimit` when jobs are independent and short-lived;
prefer a worker pool when workers hold a resource (a connection, a buffer, a
prepared statement) worth reusing.

Make every stage cancelable, and make ownership obvious from the signature: return
`<-chan T` from the function that creates and closes the channel, and accept `<-chan T`
in stages that only read.
